  relationship_status: Divorced

  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Omar, a 30-year-old tax inspector, had never imagined that a single moment could change the course of his life so dramatically. The day of the collision had begun like any other; he had been driving to work, the sun streaming through the windshield, the familiar route providing a sense of comfort. But that routine shattered in an instant when a car, swerving recklessly, collided with his vehicle. The deafening sound of metal crumpling and the smell of gasoline filled his senses as time seemed to stretch impossibly. He could still recall the panic in the eyes of the other driver, the chaotic blur of flashing lights, and the intense feeling of vulnerability that enveloped him. As he sat in the passenger seat of an ambulance, he felt his world tilt, a deep-seated belief forming that he could never trust himself again behind the wheel.

In the months that followed, Omar's life transformed. He found himself avoiding driving at all costs; even being a passenger became unbearable. Each time he stepped into a car, the memories of that day surged back, making his heart race and his palms sweat. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of handling the simple act of driving, an activity that had once defined his independence. Instead, he spent long hours glued to his phone, scrolling through social media and playing games, desperately seeking distractions from the intrusive thoughts that plagued him. The digital world provided a temporary escape, but the reality of his situation loomed large, casting a shadow over each moment of reprieve.

The effects of this avoidance began to seep into other areas of his life. His colleagues noticed that he was withdrawing, refusing invitations for lunch or after-work gatherings. He began undereating, finding it easier to skip meals than to confront the emotions that had become foreign to him. He felt disconnected from the vibrant man he once was, convinced that he would never again experience the full spectrum of emotions. Friends expressed concern, but Omar brushed off their worries, convinced they could not understand the depths of his despair.

As he moved through his daily routine, the world felt fraught with danger. Unexpected sounds sent him into a spiral of hypervigilance; the simple creak of a door or the sudden honk of a car horn would cause him to jump, his heart racing as if he were back at the scene of the accident. He was perpetually on guard, scanning his environment for potential threats, a habit that left him exhausted. He had come to believe that he couldn’t rely on himself anymore, that he was a shell of the man he had once been, trapped in a cycle of fear and anxiety.

What frightened Omar most was the thought that he would never feel "normal" again. He avoided talking about the collision with family and friends, fearing their sympathy would only serve as a reminder of his perceived inadequacies. He felt lost in the quiet of his own mind, the vibrant emotions he once felt replaced by a dull ache that made him question his self-worth. Each night, as he lay in bed, memories of the crash replayed like a haunting film, pushing him further into isolation and despair. 

It was only when he found himself unable to focus at work, staring blankly at tax forms that had once seemed straightforward, that he realized he could no longer navigate this alone. A sense of urgency washed over him; he knew he needed help. The thought of confronting his trauma terrified him, yet the prospect of continuing to live in this self-imposed prison felt even worse. He hoped that therapy could help him reclaim some sense of control over his life and emotions, but he was also terrified that he might discover he was irreparably broken. As he sat in the waiting room for his first appointment, Omar held onto a flicker of hope—that perhaps, with support, he could find a way back to himself.
